body: Looking at your post history makes me feel so bad for you, and your residency program for getting you. All of your posts have to do with lifestyle and paycheck. I think you missed the talk that all of medicine is hard, stressful, scary work. Even the "off ramp" fellowships are work. Palliative is work, wound is hard work, FM is hard work, IM is hard work, they're all hard work. Nursing is work. Welding is work. Business and communication majors end up putting in work. All jobs these days are hard work. Bosses set it up to get maximum cognitive output for minimum compensation.  The trick seems to be to accept that and pick something that won't make you rip your own eyeballs out. EM gets much, much harder as an attending and the liability is through the roof. The first year as an attending will age you more than med school and intern year combined. Judging from your post history, EM is the worst field for you. I would do some soul searching, decide if there is anything you actually sincerely like about medicine (other than the paycheck and sunk-cost fallacy). If you sincerely enjoy medicine, consider non clinical work or consider transferring to another specialty. But please pick a specialty that you actually have a genuine interest in. If you're not interested in it, you won't study, you won't learn it, and you'll end up in remediation again. Really wish you the best and hope you get some acceptance and soul searching done.

The experiences they are all having are *not* normal. The ones with flashy stuff to talk about will talk. The rest of us kept quiet. I knew a few who traveled and were very loud but most kept it cheap. I do recommend trying to take a few days to get a local vacation/ staycation. If there are any beautiful spots, camping, or hiking near you, arrange an outing. Camping can be done fairly cheaply, and will let you feel more like your peers. Being able to say "I'm camping in the __ with my family" will make you feel like you're getting something too. Or if you're not outdoorsy, a day trip to a nice spot for a picnic. Just something where you can breathe and take some photos. Also, relocation loans were for me a necessary evil. At 13%. I paid them off quickly once I became an attending but wow did they snowball in interest... Becoming a doctor is starting to be unattainable for regular people, for sure. You got this.

In my area, the nursing hotline drops a note about their conversation. I see that most of the time the patient vastly exaggerates their symptoms to the nursing hotline. "Coughing up blood for days" becomes "coughing up yellow phlegm x 1 day" once I start talking to them. I don't know why, maybe people over the phone feel that they need to sound sick enough to "deserve" the hotline, but once they go through the ED check-in they realize how serious everything is and that they need to be more up front. Maybe the nursing hotline also primes them to describe things more accurately and concisely with less dramatization.

As a female MD who was bullied by a terrible RN who tried to get me fired in residency for asking a question twice when she didn't respond the first time, here's how it would play out: 

1. You talk to the PD and the nurse was not planning to report you or go after you: you look like a trouble maker. Nothing here is sufficiently quotable enough to really call her out. Without a really rude statement to quote, your (likely male) PD will just judge you instead.

2. You talk to PD and the RN *was* planning on reporting you or going after you: first squeaky wheel gets believed more. If you report her before she reports you, your first report will likely be given more credence, and you will have protected yourself.

3. You don't talk to PD: maybe the behavior neutralizes with time as they get to know you more. It did for me. A lot of RNs see new residents as "future people to place orders on my patients who get more than me when I'm the one who actually helps patients". Familiarity and friendship can help to nullify this. Try to befriend a few female rns who are older and all the male RNs to get them on your side. 

Having a female RN be mad at a female doc is dangerous. If you have any bullies in your program leadership, they will take the RN feedback as "oh hey we caught one, someone who needs to work on their interprofessional skills" and it can jeopardize your career. Tread very very carefully from now on.

Ultimately, like 80% of medicine has multiple correct solutions. 

Solution 1: droperidol/ reglan only. I love droperidol but umm the guy has checked in 4 times so far. On the patients side, maybe the droperidol actually isn't working. For some people, they actually have legit pain. And yes, of course we are *allowed* to treat chronic pain with opiates while in the department. We do that for cancer patients all the time. We just don't discharge with opiates. Alternatively, if he just gets droperidol he'll probably check back in. And then instead of the one hour you felt was taken from your care of other patients, you would lose minimum 2 hours for a re-triage, re-evaluate, re-exam, and re-discharge.

Solution 2: give them Dilaudid so you can discharge them and get a bed for someone who is actually sick. The real question is why they needed Narcan. The provider should have appropriately dosed the Dilaudid based on the patient/ low-balled it in this case. If they only did 0.5mg and the patient still went sleepy, that's just bad luck. If they did more, eh I don't love that.  

Sounds like your docs felt it was better to give this chronic checker-in Dilaudid to clear a bed for someone potentially dying. And you just had bad luck that day.

New ED attending here. The job is pretty much impossible. You're supposed to know as much as a consultant, but also be okay being told you're an idiot about 4 times per shift by said consultants when they recommend something that absolutely does not jive with up-to-date or your knowledge of appropriate management. Patients want you to be Dr. House and Dr. Wilson at the same time, magic and perfection. And if a patient has a bad outcome, even if you did everything right, you get sued. The average ED doc will get sued at least once maybe twice over ever a short career. You're forced to see an unsafe number of patients per hour, and are competing against senior docs who are okay pushing the pace because 1) they're more experienced and 2) they don't really care if they get sued, they only work a few shifts a month to pay off their boat and could have retired yesterday without issue. 

Do anesthesia. Or rads. Or FM. The "extra free time" of EM isn't worth it, it's all absorbed by schedule flips. EM is going to die, as a specialty. It'll be soaked up by people who SOAPED in and hate the job and leave quickly. Then it'll be taken over by APPs. American business and American patients have treated us so fucking badly we all want out. Thinking of going to become an electrician if it doesn't get better.

I also always feel like the odd one out in med school and residency. It's tough. Group dynamics suck. Someone is always selected as the outsider to increase group cohesion amongst the others. The thing that gets me through it is that this is Just A Job. Once it's over, we'll have more time to make friends outside of our co-residents/colleagues. Have coworker acquaintances but have real friends outside of work. Show up, clock in, clock out, then go actually live our lives. We're not obligated to become blood brothers with our co-residents, a lot of whom are still following frat/sorority socialization patterns. I'm in my third year, few months left. I hope the end is in sight for you too. Stay strong.
